newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic said to tear up free press manifesto.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic said to tear up free press manifesto.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, who is facing mounting pressure at home and abroad, tore up a draft memorandum on press freedom presented to him to sign, an envoy of a U.S.-based journalists' rights group said on Sunday.

Milosevic subsequently signed a shortened statement indicating he supported a free press, but that version stopped short of ruling out state censorship, Kati Marton, visiting head of the U.S. Committee for the Protection of Journalists, said.
Marton is the wife of former U.S. mediator Richard Holbrooke, who secured last year's Dayton peace accord ending the Bosnian war.

Belgrade and several major Serbian cities have been shaken by three weeks of demonstrations after Milosevic's ruling Socialists annulled a victory by the opposition in 15 cities, including the capital, in local elections last month.
Marton said she felt Milosevic would not yield to opposition demands to resign and seemed instead to be prepared to outlast the daily demonstrations.
"I think he feels he has the support from the countryside so he can ride it out. I don't think that he is in a mood to give up. Not at all," she added.
Marton had travelled to Belgrade to press Milosevic to allow freedom of the press after authorities shut down independent radio B-92, the only domestic electronic media covering the demonstrations.
"I came the very minute I heard of shutting down of radio B-92 to send a very clear message of solidarity," she said.
She added that she had presented a manifesto to Milosevic listing specific methods of media control "which I wanted him to sign and pledge not to repeat ever again".

"I handed that document to him and told him that it would go a very long way towardsmending his image in the West which I told him was quite good a year ago but was now about as bad as can be," she said.

"So I handed him that manifesto which he proceeded to tear up. What is left of that manifesto is half the page that I then proceeded to write on in my own hand because I did not want to lose this opportunity, because I wanted to come away with something concrete, something in writing."
Milosevic signed that document, which reads:

"In our conversation today, Pres S.M. and I K.M. reiterated our support of a free press in the Fed. Rep. of Yugoslavia and the right to publish (underlined) + broadcast (underlined) without censorship (both words deleted) free here."
Asked who crossed out the words "without censorship", Marton replied: "It was President Milosevic."
She repeated Milosevic's promise that he would not use force to muzzle the country-wide protests.

"We are seeing history being made here in the streets of Belgrade and I commend the peaceful and even good-humoured and very dignified way in which it is being carried out and I applaud your courage," she said.
